title: Volumetric Analysis

toc.title: 8.1 Equivalent weight and every concentration unit
8.2 Primary and secondary standards; the law of equivalence

html:
Volumetric analysis is the branch of the paper where chemistry becomes a measurement: a solution of known strength is run from a burette into a measured volume of the unknown until the reaction is just complete.

It carries about one question, and that question is nearly always arithmetic — an equivalent weight, a conversion between two concentration units, or a titration volume from N_1V_1 = N_2V_2.

The definitions are few; the marks are lost on units, on the n-factor of the reagent, and on the difference between molality and molarity.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Equivalent weight E = M/n, where the n-factor is the basicity of an acid, the acidity of a base, the total charge of the cation of a salt, or the number of electrons gained or lost by an oxidant or reductant.
  • KMnO₄ has three n-factors: 5 in acidic medium (to Mn²⁺), 3 in neutral (to MnO₂), 1 in strongly alkaline (to MnO₄²⁻). K₂Cr₂O₇ is always 6.
  • Molarity = mol solute per litre of solution; molality = mol solute per kg of solvent; normality = molarity × n-factor.
  • The one conversion that needs the density: M = \dfrac{10 \times \%\text{w/w} \times d}{M_B}.
  • ppm = mg per kg (≈ mg L⁻¹ in dilute water), ppb = μg per kg; mole fraction = n_i/\sum n.
  • Dilution: M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 — the number of moles does not change.
  • A primary standard is pure, stable, non-hygroscopic and of high molar mass (oxalic acid, Na₂CO₃, KHP, borax, K₂Cr₂O₇); NaOH, HCl, KMnO₄ and Na₂S₂O₃ are secondary and must be standardised.
  • Law of equivalence: N_1V_1 = N_2V_2; equivalents = NV(\text{L}) = \text{mass}/E. In a back titration the excess is subtracted.

8.1 Equivalent weight and every concentration unit

What a titration is

Volumetric analysis

Volumetric analysis is the quantitative determination of the concentration of a solution by measuring the volume of another solution of known concentration that reacts with it completely.

Term Meaning
titrant the solution of known concentration, run from the burette
analyte (titrand) the solution being measured, pipetted into the conical flask
standard solution a solution whose concentration is accurately known
equivalence point the point at which the reactants have combined in the exact stoichiometric ratio
end point the point at which the indicator changes colour — the observed approximation to the equivalence point
titration error the difference between the end point and the equivalence point

The whole method rests on one measurement: the volume delivered. Everything else is a conversion from that volume to an amount of substance.

Equivalent weight and the n-factor

Equivalent weight

The equivalent weight E of a substance is the mass of it that supplies, consumes or is associated with one mole of H⁺, one mole of OH⁻ or one mole of electrons in the reaction concerned.

E = \frac{M}{n}

where M is the molar mass and n is the n-factor (the number of equivalents per mole).

The n-factor is not a property of the substance alone — it is a property of the substance in a particular reaction. That is why KMnO₄ has three different equivalent weights.

Substance Reaction role n-factor E (g eq⁻¹)
HCl acid (basicity 1) 1 36.5
CH₃COOH acid (basicity 1) 1 60
H₂SO₄ acid (basicity 2) 2 49
H₃PO₄ acid (basicity 3) 3 32.7
NaOH base (acidity 1) 1 40
Ca(OH)₂ base (acidity 2) 2 37
Na₂CO₃ salt, 2 H⁺ accepted 2 53
NaHCO₃ salt, 1 H⁺ accepted 1 84
KMnO₄ (acidic) Mn⁷⁺ → Mn²⁺, 5 e⁻ 5 31.6
KMnO₄ (neutral) Mn⁷⁺ → Mn⁴⁺, 3 e⁻ 3 52.7
KMnO₄ (alkaline) Mn⁷⁺ → Mn⁶⁺, 1 e⁻ 1 158
K₂Cr₂O₇ (acidic) 2 Cr⁶⁺ → 2 Cr³⁺, 6 e⁻ 6 49
FeSO₄ Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺, 1 e⁻ 1 152
H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂, 2 e⁻ 2 63
Na₂S₂O₃ 2S₂O₃²⁻ → S₄O₆²⁻, 2 e⁻ for two 1 158
I₂ I₂ → 2I⁻, 2 e⁻ 2 127
The n-factor traps
  • H₃PO₄ is tribasic, so E = 98/3 = 32.7 when all three hydrogens are replaced. In a reaction that replaces only one, E = 98; only two, E = 49. Read what the equation does.
  • Na₂CO₃ with HCl to the methyl orange end point (all the way to CO₂) has n = 2 and E = 53. To the phenolphthalein end point it stops at NaHCO₃ and n = 1, E = 106.
  • Na₂S₂O₃ has n = 1, not 2, because the two sulphur atoms in one formula unit lose one electron each between them.
  • Oxalic acid as the dihydrate has M = 126, so E = 63; the anhydrous acid gives 45.
Equivalent weight from an equation

Problem. Find the equivalent weight of KMnO₄ when it oxidises oxalate in acid: 2KMnO₄ + 5H₂C₂O₄ + 3H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O. (K = 39, Mn = 55, O = 16)

Solution. Manganese goes from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺, a gain of 5 electrons per formula unit, so n = 5. M = 39 + 55 + 64 = 158, hence E = 158/5 = 31.6 g eq⁻¹. The same reaction shows oxalate losing 2 electrons per H₂C₂O₄, so its E = 90/2 = 45.

The concentration units

Unit Definition Formula
% w/w mass of solute per 100 g of solution \dfrac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}}\times 100
% w/v mass of solute per 100 mL of solution \dfrac{m_{\text{solute}}\text{ (g)}}{V\text{ (mL)}}\times 100
g L⁻¹ mass of solute per litre of solution m/V
Molarity M moles of solute per litre of solution \dfrac{n}{V(\text{L})}
Molality m moles of solute per kilogram of solvent \dfrac{n}{m_{\text{solvent}}(\text{kg})}
Normality N equivalents of solute per litre of solution \dfrac{\text{eq}}{V(\text{L})} = M \times n\text{-factor}
Formality F formula masses per litre of solution \dfrac{\text{formula mass}}{\text{L}}
ppm parts per million by mass \dfrac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}}\times 10^{6} ≈ mg kg⁻¹
ppb parts per billion by mass \dfrac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}}\times 10^{9} = μg kg⁻¹
mole fraction x moles of one component ÷ total moles \dfrac{n_i}{n_1+n_2+\dots}

Molarity from percentage and density. This is the conversion the paper actually asks, and it needs the density because a percentage is by mass while molarity is by volume:

M = \dfrac{10 \times \%\text{w/w} \times d}{M_B}

Setting up. Take exactly 100 g of solution. It contains p grams of solute (p = the percentage) and has density d g mL⁻¹.

Step 1 — the volume of 100 g. V = \dfrac{100}{d} mL = \dfrac{0.1}{d} L.

Step 2 — the moles of solute. n = \dfrac{p}{M_B}.

Step 3 — divide.

M = \frac{n}{V} = \frac{p/M_B}{0.1/d} = \frac{10\,p\,d}{M_B}

Result. M = \dfrac{10 \times \%\text{w/w} \times d}{M_B} with d in g mL⁻¹.

What it means. A percentage tells you nothing about molarity until you know how heavy the solution is. The factor 10 comes from 1000 mL ÷ 100 g.

98 % sulphuric acid

Problem. Concentrated sulphuric acid is 98 % w/w H₂SO₄ and has density 1.84 g mL⁻¹. Find its molarity and normality. (M_{\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4} = 98)

Solution. M = \dfrac{10 \times 98 \times 1.84}{98} = 18.4 mol L⁻¹. Sulphuric acid has two replaceable hydrogens, so N = 2 \times 18.4 = 36.8 N. This is why concentrated H₂SO₄ is described as "18 M" in the laboratory.

Molality of a glucose solution

Problem. A 10 % w/w aqueous glucose solution contains 10 g of glucose (M = 180) in 90 g of water. Find its molality.

Solution. n = 10/180 = 0.0556 mol; solvent = 90 g = 0.090 kg. m = 0.0556/0.090 = 0.617 mol kg⁻¹. Note that the denominator is the mass of water, not the mass of the solution (100 g). Using 0.100 kg gives 0.556, the classic wrong option.

ppm, ppb and mole fraction

Problem.(a) 0.020 g of Ca²⁺ is dissolved in 1.00 kg of water. Express this in ppm.(b) A sample contains 5 μg of arsenic per kg. Express this in ppb.(c) 36 g of water is mixed with 46 g of ethanol. Find the mole fraction of ethanol.

Solution.(a) 0.020\ \text{g} = 20 mg in 1.00 kg, so 20 ppm.(b) 5 μg kg⁻¹ = 5 ppb (1 ppb = 1 μg kg⁻¹).(c) Water: 36/18 = 2 mol; ethanol: 46/46 = 1 mol; total 3 mol. x_{\text{ethanol}} = 1/3 = 0.333. The mole fractions of all components add to 1.

Molarity, molality and normality — the three confusions
  • Molarity is per litre of solution; molality is per kilogram of solvent. Molarity changes when the solution is warmed (the volume expands); molality does not, which is why colligative-property work uses molality.
  • Normality is molarity times the n-factor, so the same solution can be 0.1 M and 0.5 N (KMnO₄ in acid). Never write "0.1 N KMnO₄" and then use 0.1 as the molarity.
  • ppm is a mass ratio, so it equals mg L⁻¹ only for dilute aqueous solutions, where 1 L weighs about 1 kg. For a concentrated or non-aqueous solution the two differ.

Dilution

Diluting a solution adds solvent but not solute, so the number of moles is unchanged:

M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 \qquad N_1V_1 = N_2V_2

Diluting an acid

Problem. What volume of 2.0 M HCl is needed to prepare 500 mL of 0.10 M HCl?

Solution. V_1 = \dfrac{M_2V_2}{M_1} = \dfrac{0.10 \times 500}{2.0} = 25 mL. Measure 25 mL of the concentrated acid into a 500 mL volumetric flask and make up to the mark with water. (Acid into water, never water into acid.)

8.2 Primary and secondary standards; the law of equivalence

Primary and secondary standards

Primary standard

A primary standard is a substance pure enough and stable enough to be weighed directly and dissolved to give a solution of accurately known concentration, without standardising it against anything else.

Quality of a primary standard Why it matters
very high purity (99.9 % or better) the mass weighed is the mass of the substance
stable in air — not hygroscopic, not efflorescent, not oxidised the mass does not drift while you weigh it
high molar mass a weighing error of 1 mg is a smaller fraction of a larger mass
readily soluble in water it must dissolve completely and quickly
reacts rapidly and stoichiometrically a sharp end point, a known equation
non-toxic and reasonably cheap it is used in every laboratory
Primary standards Used to standardise
oxalic acid H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O NaOH, KMnO₄
anhydrous sodium carbonate Na₂CO₃ HCl, H₂SO₄
potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP) NaOH
borax Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O HCl
potassium dichromate K₂Cr₂O₇ Na₂S₂O₃, Fe²⁺ solutions
sodium chloride NaCl AgNO₃
pure zinc or copper EDTA, iodine
Mohr's salt FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇
Secondary standard

A secondary standard is a solution whose concentration is found by titrating it against a primary standard. Its own solute is not pure or stable enough to be weighed directly.

Secondary standard Why it cannot be a primary standard
NaOH, KOH hygroscopic; absorb CO₂ from the air, so the effective concentration drifts
HCl, H₂SO₄ HCl is volatile; both absorb water and their strength varies
KMnO₄ decomposes slowly, oxidises water and traces of organic matter; light-sensitive
Na₂S₂O₃ decomposes in acid and is attacked by CO₂ and bacteria; concentration falls with time
I₂ volatile and slightly soluble in water; solutions change strength on standing
"Pure" is not the same as "primary"

Analytical-grade NaOH is sold as pure pellets, yet it still cannot be a primary standard, because it takes water and CO₂ out of the air the moment the bottle is opened.

Purity at the factory and stability on the balance are different requirements, and the paper tests the second one.

The law of equivalence and the normality equation

Law of equivalence

At the equivalence point, the number of equivalents of the titrant equals the number of equivalents of the analyte:

N_1V_1 = N_2V_2

where N is normality in eq L⁻¹ and V is volume in the same unit on both sides.

Equivalents can be counted in three ways, and all three must agree:

\text{equivalents} = N \times V(\text{L}) = \frac{\text{mass}}{E} = n\text{-factor} \times \text{moles}

That identity is what makes normality so convenient: it removes the coefficients from the calculation.

Twenty millilitres of 0.1 N acid neutralises exactly twenty millilitres of 0.1 N base, whatever the acid and whatever the base, because "equivalent" already means "capable of reacting with one mole of the other partner".

Acid against base, by both routes

Problem. 25.0 mL of 0.100 M Na₂CO₃ is titrated with 0.200 M HCl to the methyl orange end point. Find the volume of acid used.

Solution — normality route. Na₂CO₃ has n = 2, so N = 0.200 N. HCl has n = 1, so N = 0.200 N. Then N_1V_1 = N_2V_2 gives 0.200 \times 25.0 = 0.200 \times V_2, so V_2 = 25.0 mL.

Solution — mole route. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Moles of Na₂CO₃ = 0.100 \times 0.0250 = 2.50 \times 10^{-3} mol; HCl needed = 5.00 \times 10^{-3} mol; V = 5.00 \times 10^{-3}/0.200 = 0.0250 L = 25.0 mL. Both routes agree.

A redox titration

Problem. 25.0 mL of a solution of oxalic acid is exactly decolourised by 20.0 mL of 0.0200 M KMnO₄ in acidic medium. Find the normality and the strength of the oxalic acid in g L⁻¹. (E_{\text{oxalic}} = 63)

Solution. KMnO₄ in acid has n = 5, so N = 0.0200 \times 5 = 0.100 N. N_1V_1 = N_2V_2: N_{\text{oxalic}} \times 25.0 = 0.100 \times 20.0, so N_{\text{oxalic}} = 0.0800 N. Strength = N \times E = 0.0800 \times 63 = 5.04 g L⁻¹.

Back titration

A back titration is used when the reaction is slow, when the analyte is insoluble, or when the end point is hard to see. A measured excess of a standard reagent is added, the mixture is left to react completely, and the unreacted excess is then titrated:

\text{equivalents used by the sample} = N_1V_1 - N_2V_2

where N_1V_1 refers to the excess reagent added and N_2V_2 to the unreacted part.

Back titration of impure limestone

Problem. 1.20 g of impure CaCO₃ is dissolved in 50.0 mL of 0.500 N HCl. The excess acid needs 20.0 mL of 0.250 N NaOH for neutralisation. Find the percentage of CaCO₃ in the sample. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16; E_{\text{CaCO}_3} = 50)

Solution. Equivalents of HCl taken = 0.500 \times 0.0500 = 0.0250. Equivalents of HCl left = 0.250 \times 0.0200 = 0.00500. Equivalents used by the carbonate = 0.0250 - 0.00500 = 0.0200.

Mass of CaCO₃ = 0.0200 \times 50 = 1.00 g. Percentage = \dfrac{1.00}{1.20} \times 100 = 83.3 %. Check the arithmetic the other way: 0.0200 eq of CaCO₃ is 0.0100 mol, and 0.0100 × 100 = 1.00 g. Both routes agree because E = M/2 = 50.

Choosing the indicator

The indicator must change colour within the steep part of the titration curve, so that the end point falls as close as possible to the equivalence point.

Titration pH at equivalence Indicator
strong acid + strong base 7 phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0) or methyl orange (3.1–4.4)
weak acid + strong base above 7 (about 8.7) phenolphthalein only
strong acid + weak base below 7 (about 5.1) methyl orange only
weak acid + weak base near 7, no sharp jump none is satisfactory
KMnO₄ against a reductant — self-indicating (purple to colourless)
iodine against thiosulphate — starch (blue-black to colourless)

Practical points that come up as one-liners
  • The burette is rinsed with the titrant, the pipette with the solution it will deliver; rinsing with water would dilute the solution.
  • The conical flask is rinsed with water only — a few drops of water in the flask do not change the number of moles present.
  • Air bubbles in the burette tip must be removed before the initial reading; a bubble that escapes during the titration makes the volume read too high.
  • Read the burette at the bottom of the meniscus, with the eye level with the reading.
  • The last drop is added dropwise, and the flask is swirled after each addition.

Formula and fact sheet

Quantity Relation
Equivalent weight E = M/n; equivalents = \text{mass}/E
n-factor: acid basicity (replaceable H⁺): HCl 1, H₂SO₄ 2, H₃PO₄ 3
n-factor: base acidity (OH⁻): NaOH 1, Ca(OH)₂ 2, Al(OH)₃ 3
n-factor: salt total charge on the cation: NaCl 1, Na₂CO₃ 2, Al₂(SO₄)₃ 6
n-factor: redox electrons gained or lost per formula unit
KMnO₄ 5 (acid, Mn²⁺), 3 (neutral, MnO₂), 1 (alkaline, MnO₄²⁻)
K₂Cr₂O₇ 6 in acid (2Cr³⁺); E = 49
Molarity M = n/V(\text{L}); M = \dfrac{10 \times \%\text{w/w} \times d}{M_B}
Molality m = n/\text{kg solvent}
Normality N = M \times n\text{-factor}
Formality formula masses per litre; used for ionic solids such as NaCl
ppm / ppb mg kg⁻¹ / μg kg⁻¹ (≈ mg L⁻¹ for dilute aqueous)
Mole fraction x_i = n_i/\sum n; \sum x_i = 1
Dilution M_1V_1 = M_2V_2; N_1V_1 = N_2V_2
Law of equivalence N_1V_1 = N_2V_2 at the equivalence point
Back titration equivalents of sample = N_1V_1 - N_2V_2
Strength g L⁻¹ = N \times E
Indicator pH range Colour change Use
methyl orange 3.1–4.4 red to yellow strong acid + weak base
methyl red 4.4–6.2 red to yellow strong acid + weak base
bromothymol blue 6.0–7.6 yellow to blue strong acid + strong base
phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0 colourless to pink weak acid + strong base
starch — blue-black to colourless iodometric titrations
KMnO₄ itself — purple to colourless permanganate titrations

Primary standards: oxalic acid, Na₂CO₃, KHP, borax, K₂Cr₂O₇, NaCl, pure Zn/Cu, Mohr's salt. Secondary standards: NaOH, KOH, HCl, H₂SO₄, KMnO₄, Na₂S₂O₃, I₂.

Chapter summary

  • Volumetric analysis measures the volume of a standard solution needed to react completely with a measured volume of analyte; the end point is the indicator's approximation to the equivalence point.
  • Equivalent weight E = M/n; the n-factor is the basicity of an acid, the acidity of a base, the cation charge of a salt, or the electron change of an oxidant or reductant.
  • KMnO₄ has three equivalent weights because it is reduced to Mn²⁺ (n = 5), MnO₂ (n = 3) or MnO₄²⁻ (n = 1); K₂Cr₂O₇ is always n = 6.
  • Molarity is per litre of solution and changes with temperature; molality is per kilogram of solvent and does not. Normality = molarity × n-factor.
  • M = 10 \times \%\text{w/w} \times d / M_B is the only conversion that needs the density; ppm and ppb are mass ratios, and mole fractions sum to 1.
  • Dilution conserves moles: M_1V_1 = M_2V_2.
  • A primary standard is pure, stable, non-hygroscopic, soluble, fast-reacting and of high molar mass; NaOH, HCl, KMnO₄, Na₂S₂O₃ and I₂ are secondary standards and must be standardised.
  • At the equivalence point N_1V_1 = N_2V_2, and equivalents can be counted as NV, mass/E, or n-factor × moles.
  • In a back titration the equivalents used by the sample are the excess added minus the excess titrated back.
  • Choose the indicator whose transition range lies on the steep part of the curve: phenolphthalein for weak acid + strong base, methyl orange for strong acid + weak base.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (a) — An acid's n-factor is its basicity, the number of replaceable H⁺ per molecule. For a base it would be the acidity, the number of OH⁻.

2. (c) — Sulphuric acid is dibasic, so E = 98/2 = 49. Option (a) forgets the n-factor and (d) is the value for H₃PO₄.

3. (b) — Two chromium atoms go from +6 to +3, so 2 × 3 = 6 electrons are gained per formula unit. Option (a) counts only one chromium atom.

4. (d) — Mn goes from +7 to +2, so n = 5 and E = 158/5 = 31.6. Option (b) is the value in neutral medium (n = 3).

5. (b) — The carbonate ion takes two protons, so n = 2 and E = 106/2 = 53. Option (a) uses n = 1, which is right only for NaHCO₃.

6. (a) — Molarity is moles per litre of solution, not of solvent. The volume includes the solute.

7. (b) — Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, so its unit is mol kg⁻¹ and it does not change with temperature.

8. (c) — N = M \times n-factor. The n-factor is 1 for HCl, 2 for H₂SO₄ and 5 for KMnO₄ in acid.

9. (d) — ppm is 1 mg per kg (or per litre of dilute aqueous solution). Option (c) is one part per billion.

10. (a) — Mole fractions are fractions of the total number of moles, so they must add up to exactly 1.

11. (c) — Formality counts formula masses per litre and is used for ionic solids such as NaCl, which contain no discrete molecules.

12. (b) — Oxalic acid is pure, stable and non-hygroscopic. NaOH absorbs CO₂ and water, HCl is volatile and KMnO₄ decomposes.

13. (a) — NaOH is hygroscopic and absorbs CO₂ from the air, so its concentration drifts. The other three are standard primary standards.

14. (d) — At the equivalence point the equivalents of the two reactants are equal: N_1V_1 = N_2V_2. Option (a) is true only for a 1 : 1 reaction in molar terms.

15. (b) — The salt of a weak base is acidic at equivalence (pH about 5), so the indicator must change in the acid region: methyl orange.

16. (c) — The salt of a weak acid is basic at equivalence (pH about 8.7), so phenolphthalein, which changes at 8.3–10.0, is the right choice.

17.(a) — Equivalents = N \times V in litres. Option(b) gives moles, not equivalents.

18. (d) — Oxalate loses two electrons, so n = 2 and E = 126/2 = 63. Option (b) is the anhydrous value, 90/2.

19. (b) — The end point is what you observe; the equivalence point is the true stoichiometric point. The small difference between them is the titration error.

20. (c) — The purple permanganate ion is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺, so the first permanent pink tint marks the end point.

21. (a) — A high molar mass makes the weighing error a smaller fraction of the mass taken. Low solubility and volatility would both be disqualifying.

22. (d) — Rinsing with the titrant removes water that would otherwise dilute it. Rinsing with water would make the delivered concentration lower than stated.

23. (b) — Sulphuric acid has two replaceable protons, so N = 2M = 2 N. Option (c) is the value for a monobasic acid.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Explain acid-base titration, the choice of indicator and the use of primary standards, with a numerical on purity. [10]
  2. Describe iodometric and complexometric (EDTA) titrations and determine copper and the hardness of water. [10]

Model answer D1: acid-base titration and standard solutions (10 marks)

Introduction. Titration finds the concentration of an unknown solution by reacting it with a solution of known concentration (the standard solution).

The end point is the stage at which the indicator changes colour, and the equivalence point is when the chemically equivalent amounts have reacted.

Primary and secondary standards. A primary standard (anhydrous Na₂CO₃, oxalic acid dihydrate, potassium hydrogen phthalate, K₂Cr₂O₇) is pure, stable, non-hygroscopic, has a high molar mass and is soluble.

NaOH, HCl and KMnO₄ are secondary standards, which must be standardised against a primary standard.

Choice of indicator.

Titration pH at equivalence Suitable indicator
Strong acid - strong base 7 (pH jump 3 to 11) any: methyl orange or phenolphthalein
Weak acid - strong base above 7 phenolphthalein (8.3 to 10)
Strong acid - weak base below 7 methyl orange (3.1 to 4.4)
Weak acid - weak base near 7, no sharp jump no suitable indicator

An indicator is a weak acid or base whose ionised and unionised forms have different colours. It changes colour around \text{pH} = \text{p}K_{In} \pm 1.

Calculations. At the end point M_1V_1/n_1 = M_2V_2/n_2, where n is the stoichiometric coefficient, or for normality N_1V_1 = N_2V_2.

  1. Standardise HCl with Na₂CO₃ (methyl orange): Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
  2. The pH curve is nearly vertical near the equivalence point and shows which indicator is suitable.
  3. In a titration with carbonate and bicarbonate mixtures, phenolphthalein (first end point) and methyl orange (second end point) give both.

Numerical. A 25\ \text{mL} sample of NaOH needs 20.0\ \text{mL} of 0.10\ \text{M} HCl: M = \dfrac{0.10\times20.0}{25} = 0.080\ \text{M}. A 0.500\ \text{g} sample of impure Na₂CO₃ needs 40.0\ \text{mL} of 0.200\ \text{M} HCl.

Moles of HCl = 8.0\ \text{mmol}, so Na₂CO₃ = 4.0\ \text{mmol} = 0.424\ \text{g} and the purity is \dfrac{0.424}{0.500}\times100 = 84.8\%.

Conclusion. The indicator must change colour in the steep part of the titration curve, and a primary standard is needed to fix the strength of any secondary standard.

Model answer D2: iodometry and complexometric titration (10 marks)

Introduction. Iodometric titrations use iodine/iodide and thiosulphate, and complexometric titrations use the chelating agent EDTA.

Iodometry (estimation of copper). Cu²⁺ oxidises iodide to iodine and the iodine liberated is titrated against sodium thiosulphate:

2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → 2CuI + I₂ and I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻.

Starch is added near the end point as indicator (deep blue with iodine) and the end point is the disappearance of the blue colour. So one Cu²⁺ is equivalent to one S₂O₃²⁻.

Sodium thiosulphate is standardised with K₂Cr₂O₇ by the same iodometric method, because it is not a primary standard.

Complexometric titration with EDTA. EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, as its disodium salt) forms a 1:1 water-soluble chelate with most metal ions, through two N and four O donor atoms.

The titration is done in a buffer at \text{pH} = 10 (NH₃/NH₄Cl) with Eriochrome Black T as indicator: the wine-red metal-indicator complex changes to blue when EDTA takes away the metal.

Hardness of water. Temporary hardness is due to Ca(HCO₃)₂ and Mg(HCO₃)₂ and is removed by boiling or by Clark's method.

Permanent hardness is due to chlorides and sulphates and is removed by adding washing soda (Na₂CO₃), permutit (zeolite) or ion exchange. Hardness is expressed as mg of CaCO₃ per litre (ppm).

Method Titrant Indicator Analyte
Acid-base HCl or NaOH phenolphthalein, methyl orange acids, bases
Redox KMnO₄ self Fe²⁺, oxalate
Iodometric Na₂S₂O₃ starch Cu²⁺, oxidants
Complexometric EDTA Eriochrome Black T Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺

Numerical.

  • 25\ \text{mL} of a copper solution liberates iodine needing 20.0\ \text{mL} of 0.050\ \text{M} thiosulphate: \text{Cu}^{2+} = \dfrac{0.050\times20.0}{25} = 0.040\ \text{M}, or 2.54\ \text{g L}^{-1}.
  • 50\ \text{mL} of water needs 10.0\ \text{mL} of 0.010\ \text{M} EDTA. Moles of Ca²⁺ = 0.10\ \text{mmol}, so in 1\ \text{L} there are 2.0\ \text{mmol}, equal to 200\ \text{mg} of CaCO₃, a hardness of 200\ \text{ppm} (very hard).

Conclusion. Starch is added late in iodometry, and EDTA titration at pH 10 with Eriochrome Black T measures the total hardness of water.
